questions.q: How does this lesson define a system of record (SoR)?
options: Any system a user happens to log into most often during the day
The system designated as the authoritative source of truth for a specific category of data
A system that has no user interface at all
Whichever system was implemented first at the company
questions.explain: A system of record is the authoritative source of truth for a category of data -- if there's ever a dispute about the correct value, the SoR's value is the one that wins.

questions.q: Per this lesson, is Salesforce always the system of record for data that's visible on a Salesforce record?
options: No -- Salesforce can show data (like an outstanding invoice balance) for which the ERP, not Salesforce, is the actual system of record
Yes -- if a field is visible inside Salesforce, Salesforce is always authoritative for it
Salesforce is never a system of record for any data under any circumstances
Only custom fields can have a system of record other than Salesforce; standard fields are always Salesforce-authoritative
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly warns that confusing 'visible in Salesforce' with 'Salesforce is authoritative' is a common and costly mistake -- an invoice balance shown in Salesforce is still authoritatively owned by the ERP's general ledger.

questions.q: This lesson says a single Account record can have fields sourced from several different systems of record. What does it say the architecture must be precise about as a result?
options: Which specific field or fact has which system-of-record authority, not just which object as a whole
Nothing -- object-level authority assignment is sufficient and field-level precision is unnecessary
Only the Account object's Name field needs an assigned system of record
System-of-record authority can be assigned randomly as long as a decision is documented somewhere
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that authority has to be assigned per field or fact, not per object -- a single Account record can legitimately be a patchwork of fields each sourced from a different system of record.

questions.q: What does this lesson call the failure mode where two systems both independently believe they are authoritative for the same fact, with no reconciliation process between them?
options: Dueling systems of record
Field-level authority
System of engagement
Classification drift
questions.explain: The lesson names this specific failure mode 'dueling systems of record' -- it produces silent data drift that often isn't noticed until a report, invoice, or audit surfaces the mismatch.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what should a System Architect do during integration design regarding shared data between systems?
options: Allow every system that touches a piece of data to edit it freely, trusting users to manually reconcile conflicts
Explicitly name exactly one system of record for every piece of shared data and make every other system a read-only or conflict-resolved consumer of it
Avoid assigning any system of record and let each system decide for itself at query time
Always designate Salesforce as the system of record regardless of the data involved
questions.explain: The lesson's prescribed fix for the dueling-systems-of-record failure is to explicitly assign exactly one system of record per shared fact, with every other system treated as a consumer rather than an independent authority.
